title: Moses did not lose his destiny in Egypt.
paragraphs: Moses did not lose his destiny in Egypt.
He just met the version of himself that could not carry it.
That is where most people misunderstand his story.

We often think Moses became a leader at the burning bush.
But the truth is… leadership did not begin with fire.
It began with failure.
In Exodus 2, Moses sees an Egyptian beating a Hebrew. Something inside him rises—anger, justice, urgency. He steps in, kills the Egyptian, and hides the body in the sand.
At first glance, it looks like courage.
But Scripture reveals something deeper.
Moses tried to deliver people before he was ready to depend on God.
And that is a dangerous place to be.
Because calling without surrender can lead to destruction.
The next day, when Moses tries to intervene again, he hears the words that expose everything:
“Who made you ruler and judge over us?”
In one moment, his identity collapses.

His position disappears.
His confidence shatters.
His future—at least in his mind—is over.
So he runs.

Not strategically.
Not spiritually.
Just… runs.

From Egypt.
From responsibility.
From the weight of what he did.
And maybe that is where this becomes personal.

Because some of us are not running from people…
We are running from moments.

Moments we wish we handled differently.
Decisions we regret.
Versions of ourselves we don’t want to face.
Moses carried that.
And for 40 years, he lived in Midian—not as a prince, not as a deliverer—but as a shepherd.

Quiet.
Hidden.
Forgotten.
Or at least… it felt that way.
But here is the part many people miss:
God never called Moses in Egypt.
He called him in the wilderness.
Let that sink in.

The place Moses thought was his ending…
was actually where God chose to speak.

In Exodus 3, there is no crowd.
No applause.
No platform.
Just a man, a desert, and a bush that burns without being consumed.
And from that fire, God calls his name.
“Moses… Moses.”

Not “deliverer.”
Not “leader.”
Not “chosen one.”
Just… Moses.
Because before God assigns purpose, He restores identity.
And this is where everything shifts.
Moses, the man who once acted boldly, now hesitates.
“Who am I that I should go to Pharaoh?”

The same man who moved without thinking…
now feels completely unqualified.
Why?
Because the wilderness did something Egypt never could.
It stripped him of self-reliance.

It taught him silence.
It taught him patience.
It taught him dependence.
And here is the lesson most people overlook:

God did not use Moses in spite of the wilderness.
He used Moses because of it.
Those 40 years were not wasted.
They were preparation.

The desert trained his endurance.
The sheep trained his leadership.
The silence trained his listening.
So when God finally called him, Moses no longer trusted himself.
And that was exactly the point.
Because God was not looking for a man who believed in his own strength.
He was looking for a man who would rely on His.
That is why God responds to Moses’ insecurity with something powerful:
“I will be with you.”

Not “You are enough.”
Not “You’ve grown.”
Not “You’re ready.”
Just—“I am with you.”
Because the assignment was never about Moses being capable.
It was about God being present.
And that changes everything.
Some of you are frustrated because your life does not look like what you expected.

You thought you would be further by now.
You thought things would have happened already.
You thought that mistake disqualified you.
But Moses would tell you this:

Delay is not always denial.
Sometimes it is development.
You are not always buried when things go quiet.
Sometimes… you are being built.
Moses left Egypt as a fugitive.
He returned as a leader.

Not because his past disappeared—
but because God transformed his dependence.
And here is the truth that will challenge you:

You can be called and still be unprepared.
You can be gifted and still be unbroken.
You can have purpose and still need process.
Moses had all three.
And God took him through all of it.
So if you are in a wilderness season right now…

Do not rush it.
Do not resent it.
Do not mislabel it.

Because the very place you are tempted to call a setback
might be the place God is shaping the strength you will need later.
The wilderness is not where your story ends.
It is where your self-reliance does.
And when that finally breaks…
Purpose becomes clear.
So here is the question:

Are you running from your wilderness…
or allowing God to use it?

Because the difference between a fugitive and a leader
is not the absence of failure—
It is what God is allowed to do with it.
